and S. et al.; Attorney-General of Ontario, Intervenant

Toronto v. S.(T.)

(Ont. C.A.)

69 O.R. (2d) 189

[1989] O.J. No. 754

Toronto Registry No. C1712/87

ONTARIO

Court of Appeal

Tarnopolsky, McKinlay and Catzman JJ.A.

May 11, 1989.

Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms
-- Child Welfare Act, R.S.O. 1980, c. 66, ss. 35(5), (7), (8)(d), 69(15), 86(1) --
Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, ss. 2(d)
,
7
,
15(1)
.
Constitutional law --
Charter of Rights
-- Freedom of association -- Application to family relationships -- Access after adoption by birth parents -- Provincial child welfare legislation precluding orders for continued access by birth parents after children's adoption by foster parents -- Legislation not violating freedom of association -- Family relationships not protected by Charter guarantee of freedom of association --
Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 2(d)
-- Child Welfare Act, R.S.O. 1980, c. 66, ss. 38(5), (7), (8) (d), 69(15).
Constitutional law --
Charter of Rights
-- Right to life, liberty and security -- Provincial child welfare legislation requiring termination of access by birth parents after children placed with foster parents for adoption -- Legislation not violating right to life, liberty or security of the person --
Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 7
-- Child Welfare Act, R.S.O. 1980, c. 66, ss. 38(5), (7), (8)(d), 69(15).
Constitutional law --
Charter of Rights
-- Equality rights -- Provincial child welfare legislation requiring termination of access rights of birth parents after children placed with foster parents for adoption -- Legislation not violating equality rights -- Situation of birth parents not analogous to that of enumerated groups --
Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 15(1)
-- Child Welfare Act, R.S.O. 1980, c. 66, ss. 38(5), (7), (8)(d), 69(15).
Two children, a sister and a brother, had been apprehended in December of 1981, and made temporary wards of the appellant children's aid society. They had been placed in the care of foster parents when the girl was two years old and the boy three months old and had resided with them ever since. Following the apprehension of the children by the society, the birth parents, and after the parents' separation, the birth mother alone, continued to see the children approximately once a month. The foster parents desired to adopt the children but were opposed to continued access by the birth parents. In order to facilitate the adoption, the society sought permanent wardship and termination of the access rights of the birth parents. In October of 1985, in a status review hearing under the Child Welfare Act, R.S.O. 1980, c. 66 (since repealed and replaced by the Child and Family Services Act, 1984, S.O. 1984, c. 55), the Provincial Court judge ordered Crown wardship with access for each birth parent to continue at least four times yearly and beyond the adoption by the foster parents unless terminated by a court of competent jurisdiction. The Provincial Court judge concluded that s. 38(8)(d) of the Child Welfare Act, which provides that no placement for adoption shall be made until any outstanding orders of access to the child under the Act had been terminated, did not apply because there was no requirement for a physical placement, the children having been in the foster parents' home all along. The judge viewed a termination of access by the birth parents as a violation of the rights of adopted children under the
Charter of Rights
. On appeal by the society, the District Court judge ordered Crown wardship with a view to adoption and further ordered that the birth parents be denied access to the children on the grounds that the statute precluded any access after adoption. The birth mother appealed to the Ontario Court of Appeal seeking a restoration of the order of the Provincial Court judge or, in the alternative, an order of Crown wardship for long-term foster care with access by the birth parents.
Held, the appeal should be dismissed.
The Child Welfare Act requires a termination of access by birth parents when children are placed for adoption. By virtue of ss. 38(8)(d) and 69(15) pre-existing access orders must be terminated by court order before placement for adoption. The Provincial Court judge was incorrect in concluding that these provisions did not cover a deemed placement. Placement is an abstract concept, it does not necessarily indicate the moment of first physically placing a child in a particular home. It occurs when there is a coinciding of the decision that a child will be adopted with the time when the child is residing with the prospective adopting parents. The primary purpose for limiting access by birth parents is not to maintain secrecy but to promote family stability. The granting of an access order after adoption would hamper the relationship between an adopted child and the adopting parents and would put that relationship on an unequal basis with a natural child-parent relationship because decisions concerning access to the child would be made by a judicial or administrative official rather than within the family unit.
The provisions in the legislation which require a termination of access by birth parents upon placement for adoption do not violate the
Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms
. The freedom of association guaranteed by
s. 2(d)
of the Charter does not protect family relationships. The fundamental freedoms are public in nature and the Constitution is concerned with those assemblies and associations outside the intimate circle of the family. The desire of a parent to be with a child has no goal or purpose like that of associations for economic, political, religious, social, charitable or even entertainment purposes. The provisions do not violate
s. 7
of the Charter. The fact that there are places that one may not go and people who may refuse to permit others to have contact and communication with themselves and their children does not amount to a deprivation of liberty or security of the person of another who might want that contact. Nor is there a violation of equality rights under
s. 15
of the Charter since the situation of birth parents is in no way analogous to that of the groups enumerated in
s. 15(1)
.

The judgment of the court was delivered by

TARNOPOLSKY J.A.:--

I

THE PARTIES AND THE APPEAL

This appeal concerns two children: a girl, who is now nine
years old; and her younger brother, who is now seven.

In December, 1981, the children were apprehended by the
Catholic Children's Aid Society of Metropolitan Toronto ("the
society") following a scalding incident, caused by their
mother, as a result of which the girl will be permanently
scarred. On consent of all parties, the children were found to
be in need of protection and the society was granted wardship
for three months, which was continued thereafter. The children
were placed in the care of the foster parents when the girl was
two years old and her brother was three months old. They have
resided with the same foster parents ever since. Following the
apprehension of the children by the society, the birth parents,
who have since separated, and latterly the birth mother,
continued to see the children approximately once a month up to
November 10, 1987, the date of the judgment appealed from
herein.

With the passage of time the foster parents indicated their
preparedness to adopt the children, but also their opposition
to such adoption if it were accompanied with an order in favour
of the birth parents for continued access. In order to
facilitate such adoption, the society sought permanent wardship
of the children and termination of access rights of the birth
parents. In October, 1985, upon a status review hearing under
the Child Welfare Act, R.S.O. 1980, c. 66 (since repealed and
replaced by the Child and Family Services Act, 1984, S.O. 1984,
c. 55), Nasmith Prov. Ct. J. ordered Crown wardship for both
children, with access for each birth parent to continue at
least four times yearly and beyond the adoption by the foster
parents, unless terminated by a court of competent
jurisdiction.

In November, 1987, Lissaman D.C.J. allowed an appeal by the
society from Judge Nasmith's order and made an order for Crown
wardship with a view to adoption, and further ordered that the
birth parents be denied access to the children.

The children's birth mother appealed to this court, seeking
restoration of the order of Judge Nasmith or, in the
alternative, an order of Crown wardship for long-term foster
care, with access by the birth parents. Her appeal was resisted
by counsel for the society, for the children and for the foster
parents. Counsel for the Attorney-General of Ontario intervened
to respond to the constitutional issues raised by the appellant
mother. The children's birth father did not participate in the
appeal.

II

THE JUDGMENTS APPEALED FROM

(
1
) Nasmith Prov. Ct. J.

The judgment of Nasmith Prov. Ct. J. is reported at
1985 CanLII 5008 (ON PROVCT)
, 48 R.F.L.
(2d) 371.

He indicated at the outset of his reasons for judgment that
all parties favoured permanent wardship for both children and
that Crown wardship should therefore be ordered under s. 30 of
the Child Welfare Act. He stated that the dispute arose because
the society requested the termination of access by the birth
parents. At pp. 374-5 he framed the question before him to be

... whether the [society] has satisfied me with clear and
compelling evidence and on the civil standard of proof that
it is in the best interests of [the children] to have access
between them and their birth parents terminated.

From the evidence of experts in child welfare, he concluded
that there would be "some advantages" if the children were
adopted by the foster parents, as opposed to their remaining
with the foster parents in long-term foster care, but observed,
at p. 379:

Apart from the question of whether access to birth parents
must always be terminated before adoption can occur, the
benefits of adoption for [the children] in my view clearly
outweigh the disadvantages of adoption.

But more to the point is the question whether the benefits
of adoption would outweigh the risks of arbitrarily
terminating access here if that had to be done.

On that subject, he found, at p. 382, that the evidence was
"not very convincing that adoption benefits outweigh the
risks of an arbitrary cut-off of access to the birth parents",
and returned to what he called the "central question", i.e.,
"whether it is even legally necessary to terminate access
before an adoption order is signed".

He answered that question in the negative. After referring to
ss. 38(5), (7), (8)(d) and 69(15) of the Child Welfare Act, he
held that the statute did not prevent the making of an adoption
order with access, but instead only prevented placements for
adoption until outstanding access orders had been terminated.
In his view, there was in the present case no need for a
physical "placement" for adoption because the children had been
in the foster parents' home all along, and the adoption
placement would be "a mere formalization" or "a deemed
placement". As the statute contemplated types of adoption for
which there was no reference to a "placement" -- such as
adoptions by relatives or step-parents where a child "remains
in the same place and simply changes its official parents" --
and as the need for the maintenance of secrecy was irrelevant
in such adoptions (as it also was in the present case), he
concluded at p. 384 that: "In the final analysis, ... the Child
Welfare Act does not clearly preclude having both birth parent
access and adoption."

Taking the view that the statute was ambiguous on the issue,
Nasmith Prov. Ct. J. was of the opinion that reliance could be
placed on
ss. 2(d)
,
7
and
15(1)
of the
Canadian Charter of
Rights and Freedoms
as an interpretative tool and that a court
of competent jurisdiction could declare one possible
interpretation of a legislative provision inapplicable if it
were ambiguous and involved serious Charter violations, whereas
another interpretation did not. He found considerable support
in the Charter for an approach that did not extend the meaning
of "placement" in s. 38(8) to cover a "deemed" placement with
long-term foster parents, and thus dismissed the society's
application to terminate the birth parents' right of access to
the children. He summarized his conclusions on p. 389 in these
words:

To summarize, in my opinion it is not appropriate or
necessary to interpret s. 38(8) of the Child Welfare Act as
precluding these children being adopted by the foster parents
while continuing to have access to the birth parents. Such an
interpretation would reinforce a serious and unjustifiable
abrogation of the
Charter
rights of adopted children. Without
that interpretation, the only valid argument for terminating
birth parent access vanishes.

If I am wrong about s. 38(8), then it is an absolute ban on
continuing access with adoption except for family adoptions
under s. 73(2).

In that case, it is a flagrant and unnecessary violation of
the
Charter of Rights
which is not justifiable in a free and
democratic society.

Finally, on the assumption that the
Charter
could not be
relied upon to reach this conclusion, he returned to the
question whether it had been demonstrated to be in the "best
interests" of the children to have birth parent access
terminated and, at p. 389, expressed his opinion that:

[W]hat the evidence does show is that it would be in the
best interests of [the children] to be adopted by the foster
parents without an arbitrary termination of their birth
parent access.

If s. 38(8) were a block to continuance of an access order
through the adoption, my view of the facts of this case is
that the adoption should be arranged with continuing informal
access.

In the result, as noted above, Nasmith Prov. Ct. J. ordered
Crown wardship for both children, with access for each birth
parent at least four times yearly, and to continue beyond the
adoption by the foster parents unless terminated by a court of
competent jurisdiction.

(
2
) Lissaman D.C.J.

The judgment of Lissaman D.C.J. is reported at
1987 CanLII 8281 (ON HCJ)
, 10 R.F.L. (3d)
343.

At the appeal the District Court judge was presented with the
evidence from the status review hearing, a follow-up assessment
by the social worker who prepared the original assessment, and
the further evidence of the social worker, the birth parents,
and the birth father's companion.

In his reasons for allowing the appeal, Lissaman D.C.J.
indicated that the first issue to be decided was whether
Nasmith Prov. Ct. J. had erred in holding that he had
jurisdiction to make the disposition which he did. After
reviewing the reasoning in the court below and referring to a
number of case authorities, Lissaman D.C.J. concluded, at p.
348:

The trial judge has in this case held that there is an
ambiguity in the sections of the statute which govern this
matter and his interpretation has led to this appeal ... I
can find no legal justification for the interpretation
adopted by Judge Nasmith and therefore propose to set aside
his order of 24th October, 1985.

In an addendum to his reasons, Lissaman D.C.J. said, in
elaboration of this conclusion:

In setting aside Judge Nasmith's Order, I have found on my
interpretation of the law that there can be no access after
an adoption has taken place and that a judge cannot make an
Order for access to survive adoption.

In my view if access by birth parents is of great
importance then an adoption order should not be made except
in cases where the benefits of adoption greatly exceed the
benefits of access.

In his reasons he then turned to the question of the
appropriate order to be made and to an examination of the
evidence with a view to determining what order was in the best
interests of the children. Following that examination, at pp.
349-50 he stated his task to be:

Having decided that access must cease if the order sought
by the [society] is made, I must decide what order will serve
the best interests of the ... children. I, because of the
position I have taken with respect to jurisdiction, do not
have available the options that Judge Nasmith found he had.
If, on reviewing all the evidence before me both old and new,
I find that access to the birth parents is in the interests
of the ... children then the appropriate order will be Crown
wardship with access.

He expressed his conclusion as follows at p. 350:

Access to the ... children by the birth parents is very
important but what is more important is the overall welfare
of the ... children. In my opinion the best interests of the
... children dictate very strongly that they should be
adopted by the [foster parents] and be free of complications
caused by the continued involvement of the birth parents. My
opinion would be the same even if I was able to order
continued access to the birth parents and at the same time
set the stage for adoption by the [foster parents].

Accordingly, as noted above, he allowed the appeal and
ordered Crown wardship with a view to adoption and denied the
birth parents access to the children.

Lissaman D.C.J. did not deal with the
Charter
arguments. His
reasons indicated that he refrained from doing so because of
his understanding of the agreement of counsel that if he were
to find, as ultimately he did, that Crown wardship leading to
adoption, without access, was in the best interests of the
children, he would not have to deal with the submissions of
counsel that the provisions of the Child Welfare Act and its
successor statute offended various sections of the Charter.

III

THE ISSUES

Although this is not the order in which they were presented,
I think the issues can best be stated as follows:

(1) Is there such ambiguity in the Child Welfare Act (and its
successor the Child and Family Services Act) as to permit the
court on a status review hearing, which is considering an
application for Crown wardship with a view to adoption by
foster parents, to grant birth parents access which is to
continue even after such adoption?

(2) If there is no ambiguity and the statute does require a
denial to the birth parents of access to the children, are such
provisions contrary to
ss. 2(d)
,
7
or
15(1)
of the
Canadian
Charter of Rights and Freedoms
and not reasonable limits under

s. 1
thereof?

(3) Could the appellate judge have overruled the reviewing
judge and decided that it was in the "best interests" of the
children in this case that there should be a placement with a
view to adoption rather than a continuation of Crown wardship
with access?

(1) Is there ambiguity in the legislation so as to permit the
ordering of continuing access by birth parents to children
adopted by foster parents?

The provisions in the Child Welfare Act (C.W.A.) that were
referred to by either of the judges appealed from or suggested
as being relevant in the course of the appeal are:

38(5) Before making an order under subsection (1) or (2)
terminating an order for access to the child made pursuant to
section 35, the court shall consider whether the benefit to
the child of any plan proposed for the child, including plans
for seeking an adoption placement for the child, outweighs
the benefit to the child of maintaining the access rights.

. . . . .

(7) Subject to sections 39 and 42, where a child has been
committed as a ward of the Crown, the order made under
paragraph 3 of subsection 30(1) shall remain in effect and
the Crown wardship shall, subject to an adoption order being
made with respect to the child under Part III, not be
terminated by, reviewed in or otherwise brought before the
court and an order of access to the child shall not be made
or applied for where the child has been placed for the
purpose of adoption in the home of a person who has been
approved by a society or by a Director as a suitable person
to adopt the child and while the child is residing in that
person's home.

(8) The placement for the purpose of adoption of the child
referred to in subsection (7) shall not be made until ...

. . . . .

(d)  any outstanding order of access to the child under this
Act has been terminated,

. . . . .

69(15) Upon the placement of a child under eighteen years
of age by an adoption agency or licensee under subsection
60(5) for the purpose of adoption, and upon the giving of all
the consents required under subsection (2), any outstanding
order of access with respect to the child, other than an
order of access made under this Act, shall terminate.

(16) No person,

(a)  who has consented to an order for adoption in
accordance with this Act;

(b)  whose consent a court has dispensed with in accordance
with this Act; or

(c)  who is a parent of a Crown ward placed for adoption,

is entitled to receive notice of the proposed adoption.

. . . . .

72. The court may make an order for the adoption of any
child resident in Ontario upon application therefor being
made in the prescribed manner by a person resident in
Ontario.

. . . . .

83. Subject to section 84, an order granting an adoption
shall be final and irrevocable and shall not be questioned or
reviewed in any court of competent jurisdiction by way of
injunction, declaratory judgment, certiorari, mandamus,
prohibition, habeas corpus or application for judicial
review.

. . . . .

86(1) For all purposes, as of the date of the making of an
adoption order,

(a)  the adopted child becomes the child of the adopting
parent and the adopting parent becomes the parent of the
adopted child; and

(b)  the adopted child ceases to be the child of the person
who was his or her parent before the adoption order was made
and that person ceases to be the parent of the adopted child,
except where the person is the spouse of the adopting parent,

as if the adopted child had been born to the adopting parent
and all the rights and responsibilities of a legal guardian
of the child that have vested in any adoption agency pursuant
to subsection 69(3) are terminated.

In considering these provisions it is important to adopt the
suggestions of counsel for the respondent society to the effect
that reference should also be made to the comparable provisions
in the successor Child and Family Services Act (C.F.S.A.). This
reference is necessary because, although the C.W.A. applied at
the time of the review hearing and, by s. 208(2)(d) of the
C.F.S.A., continues to apply to any appeal proceedings
therefrom, by cl. (e) of the same subsection, any subsequent
application for an adoption order would have to be made in
accordance with the new legislation. In comparing the two
statutes it is helpful to use the "Table of Concordance"
suggested by the respondent society:

s. 152(1), (2)

At the review hearing Nasmith Prov. Ct. J. summed up the
effect of s. 38(5), (7) and (8)(d) as carrying "a strong
implication that there is a legislated Hobson's choice between
adoption and continuing birth parent access". However, he found
ambiguity because of s. 69(15). Although I agree with him that
the relevant provisions in s. 38 require a choice to be made
and that there appears to be some conflict between that section
and s. 69(15), I also believe that the sense of s. 38 is
paramount and, like Lissaman D.C.J., I do not think that in
this particular case, the choice is difficult. It is not a
Hobson's choice.

It has to be remembered that s. 38(7) is concerned with
children who have been committed as wards of the Crown. That
section provides that once the child is placed for adoption in
the home of the person approved and is residing there, an order
for access cannot be applied for or made. However, what of pre-
existing access orders? Clearly, by either s. 38(8)(d) or s.
69(15) any such orders would have to be terminated by court
order before placement for adoption. There may be other access
orders which, by s. 69(15), terminate automatically upon
placement, but, as a result of s. 69(15), those made under the
C.W.A. would have to be terminated by court order when a
decision is made that a Crown wardship is to be replaced by an
adoption. The comparable provision in the C.F.S.A., s. 137(1),
is more explicit in providing that the access order which does
not terminate automatically is one which is made under the
child protection part of the Act. This is repeated in s. 134(2)
(a) of the C.F.S.A.

One of the reasons that Nasmith Prov. Ct. J. gave in finding
an ambiguity in the C.W.A. is that in a case such as the
present one, there is no need for a physical "placement", since
the children are already placed with the prospective adopting
parents: "The so-called adoption placement would be a mere
formalization, if you will, or a deemed placement." But I do
not see why a placement cannot include a deemed placement. The
word "placement" is not defined in the Act and, in the contexts
in which it is used, does not necessarily indicate the moment
of first physically placing a child in a particular home. It is
more an abstract concept. Placement occurs when there is a
coinciding of the decision that a child will be adopted with
the time when the child is residing with the prospective
adopting parents.

Another factor considered by Nasmith Prov. Ct. J. in
concluding that the C.W.A. did not preclude granting both an
access for birth parents and an adoption, was that secrecy was
irrelevant in this case. He referred to the majority decision
of MacKinnon A.C.J.0. in C.G.W. v. M.J. (1981),
1981 CanLII 1644 (ON CA)
, 34 O.R. (2d)
44, 130 D.L.R. (3d) 418, 24 R.F.L. (2d) 342 (Ont. C.A.), as
indicating that the purpose of limiting access by the birth
parents to the children is to maintain secrecy. However, in
that case other reasons for denying access by birth parents
were given. The whole passage, at pp. 49-50 O.R., pp. 424-5
D.L.R., should be considered:

It is hoped that adoption will ensure a safe and secure
environment for the child, the stability and continuation of
which should not be immediately threatened by access granted
to the natural parents. The new adoptive parents on their
part are given security from such upset and interference by
the secrecy provisions of the Act. Such applications for
access, if permitted, would set the secrecy provisions of
adoption orders at naught and render them meaningless. The
adoption order creates a new family: the natural parents
cease to be parents of the child and the past history of that
relationship is expunged. The adopted child becomes, in the
opening words of s. 86(1) "for all purposes" (emphasis added)
the child of the adopting parent "as if [the adopted child]
had been born to the adopting parent". The exclusion of the
history of the blood and physical relationship between the
natural parents and the child from further consideration
could not have been expressed in clearer legislative terms.

Secrecy is an important consideration, but it is not the only
one.

I agree with counsel for the respondent society that the
primary purpose indicated in the passage quoted from the C.G.W.
case, supra, is family stability. Moreover, the value of family
stability is emphasized in s. 86(1) of the C.W.A. (s. 152(1),
(2) and (3) of the C.F.S.A.). The section declares that the
adopted child becomes the child of the adopting parent and,
equally important, ceases to be the child of his or her birth
parents; and the birth parents cease to be the parents of the
adopted child. Any continuing access to that child given to
birth parents would be given to someone who is no longer a
legal parent of that child. The granting of an access order
after adoption would hamper the relationship between an adopted
child and the adopting parents. It would put that relationship
on an unequal basis with that of natural child-parent
relationships, because a judicial or administrative official
would determine who had access to the children, rather than
having that determination made within the family unit.

It follows, therefore, that the legislation (both the C.W.A.
and the C.F.S.A.) requires, in cases like the present, that
there be termination of access by the birth parents by the time
the children are placed for adoption: the choice was between
continued Crown wardship with access, or adoption with no
access for birth parents.

I note that the conclusion I have reached is not in accord
with that reached by Nasmith Prov. Ct. J. in other family law
decisions: see Children's Aid Society of Metropolitan Toronto
v. L.(J.) (1987),
1987 CanLII 8354 (ON PROVCT)
, 7 R.F.L. (3d) 329 (Ont. Prov. Ct.); Re
Catholic Children's Aid Society of Metropolitan Toronto and S.
(J.), released June 12, 1987; Re C.(T.) and Children's Aid
Society of Metropolitan Toronto, released March 23, 1984.
However, the conclusion I have reached does accord with other
decisions of lower courts -- for example, Re Children's Aid
Society of the City of Kingston and the County of Frontenac and
Theresa M., a decision of the Ontario Provincial Court, Family
Division, released January 20, 1986; Re Children's Aid Society
of Metropolitan Toronto and Joseph R. and Brenda H., a decision
of the Ontario Provincial Court, Family Division, released
October 8, 1987; H.(H.L.) v. Catholic Children's Aid Society of
Metropolitan Toronto (1987),
1987 CanLII 2361 (ON HCJ)
, 7 R.F.L. (3d) 423 (Ont. Dist.
Ct.); Re Leslie S. and Children's Aid Society of the County of
Lanark and Town of Smith Falls, a decision of the Ontario
County Court, released February 25, 1981; Re Catholic
Children's Aid Society of Metropolitan Toronto and M.B., a
decision of the Ontario Provincial Court, Family Division,
released October 28, 1983; Re B. and MacDonald and one other
application (1985),
1985 CanLII 194 (ON PROVCT)
, 29 A.C.W.S. (2d) 302 (Ont. Prov. Ct. (Fam.
Div.)).

Not having found any serious ambiguity in the Act, I do not
consider it necessary to discuss the application of
ss. 2(d)
,
7

and
15(1)
of the
Charter
as an aid to interpretation. However,
I now have to consider whether the relevant statutory
provisions contravene these Charter provisions.

(2) Are the statutory provisions requiring termination of
access upon placement for adoption in contravention of the
pertinent
Charter
provisions?

The pertinent
Charter
provisions are:

2. Everyone has the following fundamental freedoms:

. . . . .

(d)  freedom of association.

. . . . .

7. Everyone has the right to life, liberty and security of
the person and the right not to be deprived thereof except in
accordance with the principles of fundamental justice.

. . . . .

15(1) Every individual is equal before and under the law
and has the right to the equal protection and equal benefit
of the law without discrimination and, in particular, without
discrimination based on race, national or ethnic origin,
colour, religion, sex, age or mental or physical disability.

(i)  Section 2(d)

Counsel for the appellant argued that terminating the access
of the birth mother, in order to prepare for adoption in this
case, would constitute a violation of her "freedom of
association". The only authority he could refer to in support
of his proposition that this freedom applies to interpersonal
relationships like that of parent and child, is a dictum of
Kerans J.A. (the other two members concurred in the result, but
not the detailed discussion) of the Alberta Court of Appeal in
Black v. Law Society of Alberta (1986),
1986 ABCA 68 (CanLII)
, 27 D.L.R. (4th) 527,
[1986] 3 W.W.R. 590, 44 Alta. L.R. (2d) 1, at pp. 542-3:

In my view, the freedom includes the freedom to associate
with others in exercise of Charter-protected rights and also
those other rights which -- in Canada -- are thought so
fundamental as not to need formal expression: to marry, for
example, or to establish a home and family, pursue an
education or gain a livelihood.

On the other hand, there have been a number of cases which
have specifically rejected claims that family relationships
were protected by the freedom of association in
s. 2(d)
of the

Charter
. For example, in Re White and Director of Child Welfare
(1985),
1985 CanLII 1229 (AB QB)
, 64 A.R. 81 (Alta.Q.B.), it was held that
s. 2
(d)
does not apply to interests of a grandparent where custody or
guardianship is at issue; in Re Downes and Minister of
Employment & Immigration
(1986), 4 F.T.R. 215 (F.C.T.D.)
, it
was held that
s. 2
(d) does not apply to a filial relationship
to prevent deportation of the father; in Horbas v. Minister of
Employment & Immigration (1985),
1985 CanLII 5559 (FC)
, 22 D.L.R. (4th) 600, [1985] 2
F.C. 359 (F.C.T.D.), it was held that the freedom of
association under the Charter does not include the right of a
citizen and his non-citizen wife to cohabit in Canada; and in
Nova Scotia (Minister of Community Services) v. S.(M.K.)
(January 19, 1989, N.S.C.A., unreported) [since reported
1989 CanLII 8854 (NS CA)
, 88
N.S.R. (2d) 418, 19 R.F.L. (3d) 75], it was held that the
freedom under Charter s. 2(d) does not include a right to
associate in a family unit so as to prevent an order committing
a child to the care and custody of the Minister.

In another case -- Shingoose v. Minister of Social Services
(1983),
1983 CanLII 2291 (SK QB)
, 149 D.L.R. (3d) 400, 26 Sask. R. 235 (Sask. Q.B.)
(leave to appeal allowed,
1983 CanLII 2150 (SK QB)
, 4 D.L.R. (4th) 765, 31 Sask. R. 75
(Sask. C.A.), but abandoned on February 19, 1984) -- the
court was concerned with a challenge to child apprehension
provisions on the basis that they infringed the freedom of
association between a mother and her child. Halvorson J. held
(at p. 403):

Even if
s. 2
(d) were designed to protect the association
between child and parent, which I doubt,
s. 1
of the
Charter

must prevail to limit this freedom. When a child is taken
into protective custody, it is because the officer has
reasonable grounds to believe the health and welfare of the
child is in immediate jeopardy. A deprivation of association
is justified in the best interests of the child. Loss of the
freedom of association in such circumstances is a reasonable
limit prescribed by law as can be demonstrably justified in a
free and democratic society.

I believe that these comments are equally applicable to our
case. However, like the courts referred to above, I would also
hold that here there is no violation of
s. 2(d)
of the
Charter
.

Although I would not suggest that the evolution of the scope
of the freedom should be limited by what has traditionally been
considered to be within that scope, at least in the early
stages of
Charter
interpretation it has to be an important
starting point. The public nature of the fundamental freedoms
has been emphasized. Not having been a totalitarian society, we
have not been so much concerned with what one may say or write
to oneself. It is the communication to others that we have
considered important to protect and on which some reasonable
limits, like the laws of defamation, have been applied.
Similarly, the issues in our history concerning freedom of
religion have not been concerned with the private conscience of
the individual, as much as with public manifestation of it by
individuals or the collective expression of it. The freedoms of
assembly and association are necessarily collective and so
mostly public. Our constitutional concerns have not been with
assemblies within families or associations between family
members. Rather, the protections we have been concerned with
are for those assemblies and associations that take us outside
the intimate circle of our families. The family is a
collective, but the desire of one family member to associate
with another is not so much for the purpose of pursuing goals
in common, nor even pursuing activities in common (Reference re
Public Service Employee Relations Act (1987),
1987 CanLII 88 (SCC)
, 38 D.L.R. (4th)
161 at p. 226, [1987] 1 S.C.R. 313 (S.C.C.), per McIntyre J.),
as it is merely because they are members of a family. A parent
and child may associate for an economic goal, for example, but
the motivation comes from their relationship, rather than a
relationship being created because of the economic motivation.
The desire of a parent to be with a child has no goal or
purpose like that of associations for economic, political,
religious, social, charitable or even entertainment purposes.
If it has any purpose it is that of loving or being loved, of
comforting and protecting, or being comforted and protected.
That may be a right that must be protected, as in the
International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights, in which
art. 22 deals with freedom of association, while art. 23(1)
provides that:

23(1) The family is the natural and fundamental group unit
of society and is entitled to protection by society and the
State.

In adoption cases a new family is created and that new family
got protection under the C.W.A. and now gets it under the
C.F.S.A. Between its members decisions are made, as in any
natural family, as to who may come into the home and who may
not.

(ii)  Section 7

We decided that we did not need to hear the respondents on
this
Charter
challenge. It is true, as counsel for the
appellant submitted, that ever since the decision of the
Supreme Court of Canada in Reference re s. 94(2) of the Motor
Vehicle Act (1985),
1985 CanLII 81 (SCC)
, 24 D.L.R. (4th) 536, 23 C.C.C. (3d) 289,
[1985] 2 S.C.R. 486, s. 7 is not limited to procedural
guarantees. It extends, as well, to provide a basis for
challenging substantive provisions. However, I do not see how a
termination of access to a Crown ward because of adoption
deprives the birth parent of any one of life, liberty, or
security of the person.

Clearly, such termination is not a deprivation of life. I do
not see, either, how it can constitute a deprivation of liberty
or security of the person. No one has a right to go everywhere.
Outside one's own living premises there are limitations
concerning where people may go, even in many public places and
certainly with respect to the living premises of others.
Barring a person from having access to a particular person is
not a confinement. The fact that there are places one may not
go and people who may refuse to permit others to have contact
and communication with themselves or their children, does not
amount to a deprivation of liberty or security of the person of
another who might want that contact.

There is no deprivation of life or liberty or security of the
birth parents in having access to their natural children
terminated with a view to having those children adopted by new
parents.

(iii)  Section 15

A copy of the decision of the Supreme Court of Canada in
Andrews v. Law Society of B.C. released February 2, 1989 [since
reported
1989 CanLII 2 (SCC)
, 56 D.L.R. (4th) 1, [1989] 1 S.C.R. 143, [1989] 2
W.W.R. 289], arrived at our court while this appeal was being
argued. We therefore had to adjourn further arguments on s. 15
to a later date because we had just expressed disapproval of
the appellant's submissions on the ground that the birth
parents and the adopting parents were not "similarly situated".
This was the test, as acknowledged by McIntyre J. in the
Andrews case, which had been widely used by both trial and
appeal courts in this country.  It was a test derived from
Joseph Tussman and Jacobus tenBroek, "The Equal Protection of
Laws" (1949), 37 Calif. L. Rev. 341. Two interesting sidelights
are that: (1) tenBroek was born in Alberta, became blind as a
child, founded the National Federation of the Blind in 1940 and
was its president for the next 21 years; (2) the article was
selected in 1984 for inclusion as one of 22 in Great American
Law Reviews, edited by R.C. Berring and published by the Legal
Classics Library.   The "Case Note" by M. David Lepofsky and H.
Schwartz in (1988), 67 Can. Bar Rev. 115, referred to by
McIntyre J., suggested at pp. 120-1 that the Canadian courts
had taken the article "out of its jurisprudential context"
because it was written prior to Brown v. Board of Education,
347 U.S. 483 (1954), at a time when the "separate but equal"
doctrine of Plessy v. Ferguson, 163 U.S. 537 (1896), held sway.
However, the "Case Note" does not point out that the article
discredited the "separate but equal" doctrine and was an
important source (some might describe it as "seminal") for the
evolution of the doctrine's repudiation in Brown, supra. A
close reading of the article would show that Tussman and
tenBroek would have argued that, in applying the "similarly
situated" test to the Nuremberg laws of Adolph Hitler, one
would not have compared Jews with Jews, but rather German
citizens of Jewish origin with German citizens of other
origins; they would not have compared, as did the British
Columbia Court of Appeal in R. v. Gonzales (1962),
1962 CanLII 348 (BC CA)
, 32 D.L.R.
(2d) 290, 132 C.C.C. 237, 37 W.W.R. 257, Indians with
Indians, but rather the treatment of Indians who happened to
have intoxicants off the reserve with the treatment of non-
Indians who happened to have intoxicants off their
properties; and they would not have distinguished pregnant
women from all other women, as well as men, as did the majority
of the Supreme Court of Canada in Bliss v. A.-G. Can. (1978),

1978 CanLII 25 (SCC)
, 92 D.L.R. (3d) 417, [1979] 1 S.C.R. 183, [1978] 6 W.W.R. 711,
but rather would have compared the entitlement of women and of
men to unemployment insurance. However, on behalf of the whole
court in Andrews, McIntyre J. stated that that test was
"seriously deficient in that it excludes any consideration
of the nature of the law". I had thought that this court had in
fact considered the nature of the law in both R. v. Ertel
(1987),
1987 CanLII 183 (ON CA)
, 35 C.C.C. (3d) 398, 58 C.R. (3d) 252, 30 C.R.R. 209
(Ont. C.A.); leave to appeal to the S.C.C. refused (Estey,
Wilson and Le Dain JJ.) 36 C.C.C. (3d) vii,
86 N.R. 266
n, and
R. v. Turpin (1987),
1987 CanLII 6768 (ON CA)
, 36 C.C.C. (3d) 289, 60 C.R. (3d) 63, 30
C.R.R. 193. In both cases this court held that the third step
of the "similarly situated" test, i.e., the necessity of
showing "discrimination" and not merely a distinction, required
the court to have regard to both the purpose and the effect of
the legislation. This necessitated a consideration of the
nature of the law.

What test does one apply? Perhaps since McIntyre J. asserted
(at p. 12) [p. 13 D.L.R.], that "the [similarly situated]
test cannot be accepted as a fixed rule or formula for the
resolution of equality questions under the
Charter
", and since
neither my colleagues Morden J.A. in the seminal case of Re
McDonald and The Queen (1985),
1985 CanLII 162 (ON CA)
, 51 O.R. (2d) 745, 21 D.L.R.
(4th) 397, 21 C.C.C. (3d) 330 (Ont. C.A.), nor Lacourciere
J.A. in Ertel, supra, nor the court in Turpin, supra, ever
suggested that the test was the only criterion, or fixed rule
or formula, to be used to resolve equality issues under the
Charter, there is less conflict than appears at first glance.
After all, McIntyre J. did suggest that equality is "a
comparative concept, the condition of which may only be
attained or discovered by comparison with the condition of
others in the social and political setting in which the
question arises" [at p. 10].

A prior question arises, however. Is the comparison to be
made with any "others in the social and political setting in
which the question arises", or only with those others who
belong to one of the groups enumerated in
s. 15(1)
or to a
group analogous thereto? In the Andrews case, supra, McIntyre
J. suggested that: "The enumerated grounds in
s. 15(1)
are not
exclusive and the limits, if any, on grounds for discrimination
which may be established in future cases await definition" [at
p. 18]. However, in Reference re Workers' Compensation Act,
1983, (Nfld.), ss. 32, 34 released April 24, 1989 [since
reported
1989 CanLII 86 (SCC)
, 56 D.L.R. (4th) 765], La Forest J. gave this concise
and unanimous decision of the Supreme Court [at p. 766]:

We are all of the view that the Workers' Compensation Act,
1983, S.N. 1983, c. 48, which provides that the right to
compensation provided by that Act is in lieu of all rights
and actions to which a worker or dependents might otherwise
be entitled, does not, in these circumstances, constitute
discrimination within the meaning of
s. 15(1)
of the
Canadian
Charter of Rights and Freedoms
as elaborated by this court in
Andrews v. Law Society of British Columbia ... . The
situation of the workers and dependents here is in no way
analogous to those listed in
s. 15(1)
, as a majority in
Andrews stated was required to permit recourse to
s. 15(1)
.

Since "the situation" of birth parents "is in no way analogous
to those listed in
s. 15(1)
", there is no contravention of s.
15 because of the provisions in the legislation for terminating
the access rights of birth parents to children who are Crown
wards being placed for adoption.

(iv)  Section 1

In view of my conclusions on
ss. 2
(d),
7
and
15(1)
, it is not
necessary to consider
s. 1
of the
Charter
in this case.

(
3
) Could the appellate judge have overruled the reviewing
judge and decide that it was in the "best interests" of the
children to be "placed" for adoption rather than to remain as
Crown wards with the birth parents having access?

The appeal to Lissaman D.C.J. was from a status review under
s. 37 of the C.W.A. Such appeal is brought under s. 43. By s-s.
(8) thereof, the appellate court may consider new evidence:

43(8) On the hearing of the appeal and with leave of the
county or district court hearing the appeal, further evidence
relating to matters both preceding and subsequent to the
making of the decision being appealed, may be received by
affidavit, oral examination or as may be directed by the
county or district court.

As this court stated in Children's Aid Society of Renfrew
County v. L. P.W. (released February 2, 1989 [since reported
32
O.A.C. 394
]), any new evidence that "could have the effect of
altering the result arrived at by the judge appealed from", may
be admitted, but the appellate judge has "to consider this
evidence in the context of exercising an appellate function and
not a hearing de novo".

In this function the appeal judge, like the reviewing judge,
must have regard to "the best interests of the child". The
relevant factors in this determination are set out in s. 1(1)
(b) of the C.W.A.:

(b)  "best interests of the child" means the best interests
of the child in the circumstances having regard, in addition
to all other relevant considerations, to

(i)   the mental, emotional and physical needs of the child
and the appropriate care or treatment, or both, to meet such
needs,

(ii)   the child's opportunity to enjoy a parent-child
relationship and to be a wanted and needed member within a
family structure,

(iii)   the child's mental, emotional and physical stages
of development,

(iv)   the effect upon the child of any disruption of the
child's sense of continuity,

(v)   the merits of any plan proposed by the agency that
would be caring for the child, compared with the merits of
the child returning to or remaining with his or her parent,

(vi)   the views and preferences of the child, where such
views and preferences can reasonably be ascertained,

(vii)   the effect upon the child of any delay in the final
disposition in the proceedings,

(viii)   any risk to the child of returning the child to or
allowing the child to remain in the care of his or her
parent;

As indicated earlier in the discussion of the proper
interpretation of the legislation, I am of the opinion that
Lissaman D.C.J. correctly concluded that Nasmith Prov. Ct. J.
was wrong in law in holding that it was possible to combine
adoption with continued access by birth parents. When a trial
judge has erred in law, an appellate court may review the
decision appealed from. However, I think also that Lissaman
D.C.J. was right in concluding that denying birth parent access
to the children, with a view to adoption, was "in the best
interests" of the children.

For one thing, as counsel for the appellant conceded, and as
Nasmith Prov. Ct. J. acknowledged, all expert witnesses,
including the expert called by the birth parents, were in
favour of adoption. Even if one were to concede that some
experts also recognized some value to continuing access, such
recognition was placed in hypothetical contexts. Moreover, once
it has been decided that the legislation does not permit an
order for both a placement with a view to adoption and birth
parent access, the hypothetical answers lose their relevance.

The second point is that the reviewing judge, having come to
the opposite conclusion, does not seem to have considered the
choice before him, i.e., access or placement for adoption. He
could not, therefore, have considered such factors in "the best
interests" of the children, which pointed in the direction of
eventual adoption, as those set out in paras. (ii) enjoying a
parent-child relationship; (iv) the effect upon the child of
any disruption; (v) the merits of an adoption plan as opposed
to the merits of returning the children to the birth parents;
(vii) the effect upon the child of any delay. All of these
factors would have pointed in favour of adoption even at the
time of the review hearing. Today, some seven years after the
children were taken into the home of the foster parents, it is
even more clear that adoption is in the best interests of the
children.

The third point is that Lissaman D.C.J. specifically
considered both the evidence which had been before the
reviewing judge, as well as the new evidence which he ordered
in order to get an up-to-date assessment. Perhaps the most
succinct summary of the new evidence can be found in the
following passage from the report of Ms Faucher, prepared for
Lissaman D.C.J.:

Over the past almost six years, the [prospective adopting
parents] have functioned as the children's primary caretakers
and are in fact the children's psychological parents. It is
generally accepted as a tenet of family life, with the
exception of issues of children's physical or emotional
safety, that parents are allowed to raise their children
according to their accepted values. The imposition of
unwanted relationships during the children's formative years
is an unnecessary intrusion into family life. Furthermore,
the continuation of the unsettled nature of these parents'
relationship to their children, poses a potential threat to
this family's stability.

Based upon this old and new evidence Lissaman D.C.J. decided
that it was in the "best interests" of the children that an
order for Crown wardship with a view to adoption be made rather
than continuing Crown wardship with access. I agree.

IV

THE DISPOSITION

For the reasons set out in Part III, I would dismiss the
appeal.

Appeal dismissed.
